n: Joseph fell on his father’s face, weeping and kissing him. As promised in Genesis 46:4, Joseph was with Jacob at his death.
Joseph had Egyptian physicians embalm Jacob so the body could be carried to Canaan for burial.

f.g: preserve a body with spices and drying, as in Egyptian mummification

n: Embalming took forty days, and Egypt mourned seventy days—nearly the honor given a pharaoh—showing their great respect for Joseph’s family.
After the mourning period, Joseph asked Pharaoh’s court to bring his request to the king, using proper channels perhaps because he was in mourning.
Joseph explains that he swore to bury his father in Canaan and promises to return.

f.w: which I have digged for me

n: Pharaoh grants permission, honoring the oath Joseph had sworn.
An enormous funeral procession went with Joseph: Pharaoh’s officials and the leaders of Egypt.
All of Jacob’s family went too, leaving only the children and livestock in Goshen—perhaps a guarantee they would return.
Chariots and horsemen accompanied them. It was a royal-scale procession.
At the threshing floor of Atad they held a seven-day mourning ceremony with loud lamentation.

f.g: a flat open area for separating grain, often used for public gatherings
probably east of the Jordan from the writer’s viewpoint, though its location is uncertain

n: The Canaanites were so struck by this Egyptian mourning that they named the place Abel-mizraim, a wordplay meaning “mourning of Egypt” or “meadow of Egypt.”
Jacob’s sons carried out his instructions faithfully.
They buried him in the cave of Machpelah, the family tomb, in the land God had promised.

f.w: the cave of the field of Machpelah

n: After the burial, everyone returned to Egypt as Joseph had promised Pharaoh.
With Jacob gone, the brothers feared Joseph had only been kind for their father’s sake and would now take revenge. Guilt still haunted them.
They sent a message claiming their father had left instructions before he died.
They asked Joseph to forgive them as “servants of the God of thy father.” Joseph wept—hurt, perhaps, that they still doubted his forgiveness.
The brothers came and fell before him, offering themselves as slaves—the final fulfillment of Joseph’s boyhood dreams.
Joseph gently answers: “Am I in the place of God?” Judgment and vengeance belong to God, not to him.

f.w: am I in the place of God?

n: The great summary of Joseph’s life: what they meant for evil, God meant for good, to save many lives. God can turn even the worst acts of others into blessings.

f.w: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good

n: Joseph reassures them twice not to fear and promises to provide for their families. He spoke kindly—literally “to their hearts.”
Joseph lived to 110, which Egyptians considered the ideal lifespan—a sign of a blessed life.

f.g: In Egyptian texts, 110 years was the ideal full life.

n: Joseph lived to see great-grandchildren from Ephraim and Manasseh. Being raised “upon Joseph’s knees” suggests he welcomed them as his own.

f.g: Manasseh’s son, ancestor of a major clan

n: Dying, Joseph prophesied that God would “visit” Israel and bring them to the promised land. The Joseph Smith Translation greatly expands this prophecy, including words about Moses and a latter-day seer named Joseph, also quoted by Lehi in 2 Nephi 3.

f.g: God will come to help you; Moses later uses these words
JST Genesis 50:24-38 adds a long prophecy of Joseph

n: Joseph made Israel swear to carry his bones to Canaan when God delivered them. This was an act of faith: he wanted to rest in the land of promise.

f.w: ye shall carry up my bones from hence

n: Genesis ends with Joseph embalmed in a coffin in Egypt—waiting, like Israel itself, for the day God would bring His people home. The next book, Exodus, tells that story.

f.g: a chest or box; the same word is used for the ark of the covenant
